home.bio1: I'm Maxime, 20, a software engineer in Bordeaux and a third-year student at EPSI. I started playing around with computers as a kid, mostly because I liked figuring out how things work. That turned into building websites for people around me, and I never really stopped. I still learn mostly by building something and seeing where it breaks.
home.bio2: A lot of what I work on comes down to trust: knowing who you're dealing with, human or AI, and being able to check it yourself. I don't think that should depend on one company or one authority holding the list. AI agents are about to act for us all over the place, and right now nobody can really tell who an agent is or who sent it. I care about self-sovereign identity, privacy and the open web, and yes, I like web3. I'm betting my early career on this being one of the big problems of the next decade.
home.bio3: Day to day, that means Verana at 2060.io, an open trust layer for digital identity: a public registry of who is allowed to issue or verify which credentials. I build the Verana dashboard, the OpenID4VC issuer and verifier in VS Agent, and the tooling that checks whether identity wallets can actually talk to each other (often they can't). I co-wrote parts of the specs, and a few of my fixes went upstream into credo-ts at the OpenWallet Foundation. I'm also in the W3C Credentials Community Group and Trust over IP, which mostly means a lot of spec reading.
home.bio4: The rest of the week is split between a few other things. I co-founded CiteMe, where I'm CIO, which measures what ChatGPT, Perplexity and the others say about a company. I'm an apprentice at Hop Hop Immo, working on their new-build real estate platform. I run Klyx, a small web and AI studio for startups. And I've started Euthyne, which records what AI agents did and what they were allowed to do, so anyone can check. Sleep is negotiable. When I can, I'm at GDG Bordeaux meetups.

I trained competitively with the French Gymnastics Federation from 2017 to 2025, and in 2025 I co-founded PKBA, a club near Arcachon that now has more than 100 members. research.title: Research
research.intro: A few problems I keep coming back to, what I've shipped on each, and what I still don't know how to answer.

areas.title: Accountability for AI agents
areas.body: Agents now write code, call APIs and act for people. When someone asks what an agent did, the answer usually comes from logs held by whoever ran it. With Euthyne I'm working on records an outsider can check: what the agent was allowed to do when it started, and a signed receipt for each action, marked inside, outside or unknown against those permissions. Content is stored as salted hashes, receipts go into an append-only public log anchored with OpenTimestamps, and anyone can verify them offline. Coding agents come first, because that's where the question already gets asked, in security reviews and audits. The signing is the easy part. The hard part is deciding what a record can honestly prove and being clear about what it can't.

areas.title: Trust registries and wallet interoperability
areas.body: Identity wallets decide who to trust from a list baked in at build time. At 2060.io I work on Verana, a public registry of who may issue or verify which credentials. I wrote the OpenID4VC issuer and verifier in VS Agent, which refuses to proceed when the registry doesn't vouch for the other side, and I patched existing wallets to do the same lookup. I co-authored the Verana trust specifications. The preprint Conformant but Not Compatible came out of testing thirteen production wallets against each other: they pass their own conformance tests and still can't talk to one another.

areas.title: How AI engines read the web
areas.body: AI engines now describe companies to people who never visit their site, and nobody at the company is asked. At CiteMe we measure that answer and the traffic behind it. Two studies so far. The first looked at 385,057 AI-agent requests across 20 sites and found that 7% of what passes for AI crawler traffic is something else. The second shows you can tell which AI assistant fetched a page from its network calls alone, but you can only tie that to a visit when the assistant reads the page live.

questions: When an agent's permissions change mid-session, which version was it really acting under, and how do you prove it after the fact?
How much of an agent's work can you prove to an outsider without showing them the code it touched?
A live trust lookup is a network dependency. What should a wallet do when the registry is down, and does fail-closed survive real users?
Can a model ever check who is behind a claim before it repeats it about a company?
research.metaDescription: Accountability for AI agents, trust registries and wallet interoperability, and how AI engines read the web.

cv.title: Curriculum Vitae

experience.title: Founder
experience.desc: Accountability for AI agents, starting with coding agents. Building it solo: a Go CLI that captures Claude Code sessions through hooks and signs a receipt per tool call on the developer's machine, the agent's permission settings captured as a signed mandate, a public append-only log anchored with OpenTimestamps, a verifier that needs no account, and the dashboard.

experience.title: Software Engineer
experience.desc: Full-stack engineer on Verana, an open trust layer for digital identity. Built large parts of the Verana dashboard (Next.js), including the v4 redesign and the Corporation feature with governance, operator grants and fee grants. Wrote the OpenID4VC issuer and verifier plugin for VS Agent, with SD-JWT VC issuance and fail-closed trust checks. Co-authored the Verana specifications and the SD-JWT VC section of the Verifiable Trust spec. Patched trust resolution into existing identity wallets and built the conformance tooling that tests them on real devices. Fixes merged upstream in credo-ts.

experience.title: Co-founder & CIO
experience.desc: Generative engine optimization platform measuring and improving how brands appear inside AI search engines. Own data, backend direction and infrastructure: Supabase with Postgres and pgvector for retrieval, a custom job queue, the multi-provider LLM layer, and the observability and billing plumbing behind a product with paying customers.

experience.title: Software Engineer (apprentice)
experience.desc: Built Hoppy, the conversational AI assistant that helps buyers search a catalogue of 28,000+ new-build homes. Work across the Next.js site and its Java API: listing and programme pages, city pages, geo-search, financing simulators, user accounts, an in-house consent banner, and the Python agent pipeline that writes content. Internship in early 2026, freelance from March, apprenticeship since September 2026.

experience.title: Founder
experience.desc: Web and AI studio for startups and tech teams, run end to end: AI audits, sites built to be read by Google and AI engines, and assistants or agents shipped in two-week sprints. Clients include PKBA, Kenzi and Reciproq.

experience.title: Web Developer
experience.desc: Two-month engagement building key pages of the first marketing site for a French mental health startup. Next.js and Tailwind, implementing the Figma design system mobile-first, with data-driven modules for testimonials and pricing.
